**Jakarta**,[[b]](#cite_note-8) officially the **Special Capital Region of Jakarta**,[[c]](#cite_note-9) is the [*de facto* capital](/wiki/Capital_of_Indonesia "Capital of Indonesia") and [largest city](/wiki/List_of_Indonesian_cities_by_population "List of Indonesian cities by population") of [Indonesia](/wiki/Indonesia "Indonesia"), with administrative status equivalent to a [province](/wiki/Provinces_of_Indonesia "Provinces of Indonesia"). It lies on the northwestern coast of [Java](/wiki/Java "Java"), borders the provinces of [West Java](/wiki/West_Java "West Java") and [Banten](/wiki/Banten "Banten"), and faces the [Java Sea](/wiki/Java_Sea "Java Sea") to the north. Jakarta itself covers about 662 square kilometres (256 square miles), but the wider [Jakarta metropolitan area](/wiki/Jakarta_metropolitan_area "Jakarta metropolitan area")—locally known as *Jabodetabek*—is among the [largest urban agglomerations in the world](/wiki/List_of_largest_cities "List of largest cities"). It is the country's political, economic, and cultural centre and contains many national institutions, corporate headquarters, and the secretariat of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations ([ASEAN](/wiki/ASEAN "ASEAN")).

The area that now forms Jakarta has been inhabited since at least the early centuries of the Common Era and was long associated with [Sunda Kelapa](/wiki/Sunda_Kelapa "Sunda Kelapa"), the port of the [Sunda Kingdom](/wiki/Sunda_Kingdom "Sunda Kingdom"). In 1527, the settlement was renamed Jayakarta after being captured by forces of the [Demak Sultanate](/wiki/Demak_Sultanate "Demak Sultanate"). The [Dutch East India Company](/wiki/Dutch_East_India_Company "Dutch East India Company") (VOC) seized the city in 1619 and rebuilt it as [Batavia](/wiki/Batavia,_Dutch_East_I

At launch, the electric SUV was solely offered with [rear-wheel-drive](/wiki/Rear-wheel-drive "Rear-wheel-drive") and an [electric motor](/wiki/Electric_motor "Electric motor") located at the rear axle, with the dual motor [all-wheel-drive](/wiki/All-wheel-drive "All-wheel-drive") version to follow later. First sales were for the ID.4 "1st edition", which differs in some interior and exterior features from the series production models.[[19]](#cite_note-19)

In Brazil there was a campaign *Vote no Cristo* (Vote for the Christ) which had the support of private companies, namely telecommunications operators that stopped charging voters to make telephone calls and SMS messages to vote.[[14]](#cite_note-14) Additionally, leading corporate sponsors including [Banco Bradesco](/wiki/Banco_Bradesco "Banco Bradesco") and [Rede Globo](/wiki/Rede_Globo "Rede Globo") spent millions of [reals](/wiki/Brazilian_real "Brazilian real") in the effort to have the statue voted into the top seven.[[5]](#cite_note-nwVFC-5) *[Newsweek](/wiki/Newsweek "Newsweek")* reports the campaign was so pervasive that:[[5]](#cite_note-nwVFC-5)

> One morning in June, Rio de Janeiro residents awoke to a beeping text message on their cell phones: "Press 4916 and vote for Christ. It's free!" The same pitch had been popping up all over the city since late January—flashing across an electronic screen every time city-dwellers swiped their transit cards on city buses and echoing on TV infomercials that featured a reality-show celebrity posing next to the city's trademark Christ the Redeemer statue.

— Elizabeth Dwoskin, *Newsweek*

According to an article in *Newsweek*, around 10 million Brazilians had voted in the contest by early July.[[5]](#cite_note-nwVFC-5) This number is estimated as the New 7 Wonders Foundation never released such details about the campaign. After the men hauled the *Flyer* back from its fourth flight, a powerful gust of wind flipped it over several times, despite the crew's attempt to hold it down. Severely damaged, the *Wright Flyer* never flew again.[[92]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHoward1988139-95) The brothers shipped the airplane home, and years later Orville restored it, lending it to several U.S. locations for display, then to the [Science Museum](/wiki/Science_Museum,_London "Science Museum, London") in London (see Smithsonian dispute below), before it was finally installed in 1948 in [the Smithsonian Institution](/wiki/The_Smithsonian_Institution "The Smithsonian Institution"), its current residence.

The Wrights sent a telegram about the flights to their father, requesting that he "inform press".[[45]](#cite_note-WDL-45) However, the *Dayton Journal* refused to publish the story, saying the flights were too short to be important. Meanwhile, against the brothers' wishes, a telegraph operator leaked their message to a Virginia newspaper, which concocted a highly inaccurate news article that was reprinted the next day in several newspapers elsewhere, including Dayton.[[93]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrouch1989271–272-96)[[94]](#cite_note-97)

The Wrights issued their own factual statement to the press in January.[[95]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrouch1989274-98) Nevertheless, the flights did not create public excitement

During the late 1940s, Woodward synthesized many complex natural products including [quinine](/wiki/Quinine "Quinine"), [cholesterol](/wiki/Cholesterol "Cholesterol"), [cortisone](/wiki/Cortisone "Cortisone"), [strychnine](/wiki/Strychnine "Strychnine"), [lysergic acid](/wiki/Lysergic_acid "Lysergic acid"), [reserpine](/wiki/Reserpine "Reserpine"), [chlorophyll](/wiki/Chlorophyll "Chlorophyll"), [cephalosporin](/wiki/Cephalosporin "Cephalosporin"), and [colchicine](/wiki/Colchicine "Colchicine").[[8]](#cite_note-8) With these, Woodward opened up a new era of synthesis, sometimes called the 'Woodwardian era' in which he showed that natural products could be synthesized by careful applications of the principles of [physical organic chemistry](/wiki/Physical_organic_chemistry "Physical organic chemistry"), and by meticulous planning.

Many of Woodward's syntheses were described as spectacular by his colleagues and before he did them, it was thought by some that it would be impossible to create these substances in the lab. Woodward's syntheses were also described as having an element of art in them, and since then, synthetic chemists have always looked for elegance as well as utility in synthesis.
